Q: Why aren't my benchmark results faster in Release compared to Debug? A:

Disclaimer: I have not run your benchmark, so I cannot comment on the reproductability of the results (it's possible it's a machine specific issue, although that's doubtful).

As you suspect, there isn't anything the runtime can optimize in your Trim, ContainsAny and Remove methods. Usually the runtime can optimize loops but your loops are as simple and straightforward as can be. The same goes for your validations, which are just straightforward if checks. This is why you don't see any meaningful improvement in Release.

Your Substring method is another matter. Apart from calling the base Substring you do some calculations and other operations, those definitely can be optimized, which is why you're seeing a constant ~7% improvement in the "Release" run.
Just a note, though: since the vast majority of the work in that method is memory allocation - that can never be optimized by the runtime. Since (from what I got) you plan to update it with Span that is when I suspect you will see a massive improvement in the benchmark.

As for the Replace method - I don't see any method in your project that corresponds to the signature you use in the benchmark. Did you intend to pass an IEnumerable<string>?

Q: How do I update Node.js? A:

2026 Update: Use FNM

  • fnm is a fully Rust-based Node.js version manager and 10 times faster than nvm. It works on Windows, Mac, and Linux, unlike nvm

  • Check which version of fnm is installed

    fnm --version

  • Install a specific version of Node.js

    fnm install 22.12.10

  • Use a specific version of Node.js

    fnm use 22.12.10

  • Check out all the fnm commands here

Older answer with nvm

To upgrade Node.js, you may first want to see which version of Node.js you are currently using:

node --version

Find out which versions of Node.js you may have installed and which one of those you're currently using:

nvm ls

List all versions of Node.js available for installation:

nvm ls-remote

Apparently for Windows, the command would be rather like this:

nvm ls available

Assuming you would pick Node.js v8.1.0 for installation you'd type the following to install that version:

nvm install 8.1.0

You are then free to choose between installed versions of Node.js. So if you would need to use an older version like v4.2.0 you would set it as the active version like this:

nvm use 4.2

That should be all.

In 2013, I used the following instructions to upgrade from Node.js version 0.10.6 to 0.10.21 on a Mac, for more recent instructions see above.

Update from 2017: Please mind, Mr. Walsh himself recommended to update Node.js just using nvm instead.

  1. Clear NPM's cache:

     sudo npm cache clean -f

  2. Install a little helper called 'n'

     sudo npm install -g n

  3. Install latest stable Node.js version

     sudo n stable

Alternatively pick a specific version and install like this:

sudo n 0.8.20

For production environments you might want to pay attention to version numbering and be picky about odd/even numbers.

Credits

  • General procedure: D.Walsh
  • Stable/unstable versions: P.Teixeira

Q: Multiprocessing: How do sharedctypes (RawArray, RawValue) work internally, how do they compare to SharedMemory and related questions A:

TL;DR:
The differences are mainly in interface and use-case. If you want true shared memory between independent processes, RawValue/RawArray are not going to cut it. SharedMemory allows you to access the shared memory block using a friendly name.

Long Answer:

Q1 As far as I understand from this issue in the Python bugtracker, the recently introduced multiprocessing.shared_memory.SharedMemory uses POSIX named shared memory. When it comes to types like RawArray and RawValue defined in multiprocessing.sharedctypes, however, the Python docs leave much to be desired. How are they implemented internally?

The core of RawArray, RawValue and the shared memory module is mmap [1] [2].

Q2 Is the only practical difference between, say, a RawArray('B') and an instance of multiprocessing.shared_memory.SharedMemory that the latter has a name and is also accessible from unrelated (possibly non-Python) processes? Is their performance comparable?
...
This then seems very similar to how POSIX shared storage, i.e. SharedMemory works.

Yes they are similar. The main differences are:

  1. You have to manage the lifecycle of this memory.
    • RawValue/RawArray is managed. The BufferWrapper registers a "finalizer" action which will be invoked when the process terminates normally. This will end up freeing up the memory arena, closing the fd, etc (essentially doing the cleanup work for you).
    • The SharedMemory object does not do this. When the process exits, only the handles to the shared memory are destroyed. The shared memory itself will persist until some process calls unlink [3].
  2. Usage from another independent process on the same machine.

    • SharedMemory creates a named shared memory block. You can access this block from any other process on that machine using just this name. This name is the name that's passed to the shm_open system call [4]. Any other process on that same machine can similarly call shm_open with the same name while specifying O_CREAT and you'll be hitting the same block of shared memory.

    • RawValue/RawArray rely on a temporary file. If you poke into the internals [5] on how the name is generated (which you could and you could potentially use this to gain access to the contents from another process somewhere on the machine), there are a few pitfalls/ugly dragons:

      1. The name is generated by calling mkstemp which has this big caveat in the docs - "The file is readable and writable only by the creating user ID." [6]

      2. It includes the pid of the calling process. This would be extremely ugly/hacky to reference in some other process.

      3. If you're not in a Linux environment, then this is a lot worse. You'd be dealing with a file location decided by get_temp_dir [7]. This function implementation [8] has a bunch of red flags like the directory being cleaned up when the calling process exits, the OS randomly doing cleanup in the temp directory, etc.

      4. Overall this interface lends itself to a forking architecture where you want to share memory between different processes running the same code.

Q3 How exactly are multiprocessing locks implemented in Python?

The implementation for the locks in the multiprocessing library can be found here - https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/a33f2c2bae759fc9d06e1c032fd2026135f2df45/Lib/multiprocessing/synchronize.py#L46

In Linux, this is implemented using sem_open , sem_wait , sem_post , etc. [9]. These are named semaphores which are shared between processes on that machine.

EDIT: The multiprocessing library's Lock however will not be shared between truly independent processes. This is because the Lock implementation uses a randomly generated name [10]. However, if you have a forking architecture and you create this Lock in the parent process, it will be shared with the forked child processes as the name will be shared as well.

References:

  1. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/multiprocessing/heap.py#L89

  2. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/multiprocessing/shared_memory.py#L117

  3. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/multiprocessing/shared_memory.py#L238

  4. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/multiprocessing/shared_memory.py#L106

  5. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/multiprocessing/heap.py#L83

  6. https://docs.python.org/3/library/tempfile.html#tempfile.mkstemp

  7. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/multiprocessing/heap.py#L98

  8. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/multiprocessing/util.py#L211

  9. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Modules/_multiprocessing/semaphore.c#L226

  10. https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/multiprocessing/synchronize.py#L124

Q: Reproducing buffer overflow A:

Managed to reproduce with the hints from the comments.

compiling with

gcc -m32 -fno-stack-protector -fno-PIE -no-pie bof.c -o bof.out

reproducing with

./bof.out $'1234567890123456789012\xca\x91\x04\x08'

UPDATE:

Taking into an account comment to this answer:

$ nm bof.out | grep call_me
080491a0 T call_me_twice
$ ./bof.out $'1234567890123456789012\xa0\x91\x04\x08'
Example
1234567890123456789012��
Example
Segmentation fault (core dumped)

A couple of other ways to find an address of a function in the binary:

$ objdump -t bof.out | grep call_me
080491a0 g     F .text  00000019              call_me_twice
$ readelf -Ws bof.out | grep call_me
    30: 080491a0    25 FUNC    GLOBAL DEFAULT   13 call_me_twice
